Chapter 3: Why Conversations About Race Are So Difficult
Let’s be honest—talking about race can feel like stepping into a room full of unspoken secrets. In so many families and schools, the topic just sits there, silent and heavy. Adults worry they’ll say the wrong thing, so they keep quiet. And kids? Well, they pick up on that tension right away, learning to tiptoe around the subject themselves.
But here’s the thing—staying silent, even with the best intentions, usually does more harm than good.
Imagine a parent whose child comes home upset—their hair or skin was teased at school. The urge to comfort is strong, but what do you say? Should you brush it off, hoping it’s just a misunderstanding? Or should you dive into the bigger history behind comments like that, even if it feels overwhelming for your child? Most parents settle for a gentle hug and a soft promise that things will get better. But deep down, the questions don’t really go away, do they?
Teachers face these moments too. Maybe during a lesson on civil rights, a student asks, “Why haven’t things changed more?” or wonders why some neighborhoods are still so divided. You can almost see the teacher freeze, maybe steering the conversation back to safer ground, missing out on a real moment of learning. The fear of conflict, of sparking controversy, keeps so many from really diving in.
This isn’t just by accident. For generations, people have been taught that talking about race is impolite, or even dangerous. The idea of being “colorblind” gets held up as the ideal—as if not seeing differences is the same as treating everyone fairly. But let’s be real—kids aren’t fooled. They notice who gets stopped by police, who’s represented in their textbooks, and who’s missing from their classrooms.
And when conversations about race do happen, they’re often reactive—sparked by a crisis or something in the news. Suddenly, emotions are running high, and the pressure to say exactly the right thing can feel paralyzing. Some people get defensive, insisting they “don’t see color” or that “everyone has the same opportunities.” Others just go quiet, afraid of making things worse.
But when we avoid these conversations, we leave a vacuum. Kids and adults both start to fill that empty space with guesses, half-truths, and old stereotypes. If a student never hears about their own history at school, they might start to wonder if it matters at all. If a teacher never brings up race, it can send the message—maybe without meaning to—that it’s just too dangerous to talk about.
So, how do we break the silence? It takes real courage and a lot of humility. It means being honest about what we don’t know, and being open to learning. It means listening to stories—some of them uncomfortable—and recognizing the pain others might carry. Most of all, it means creating spaces where questions are welcome, and mistakes aren’t met with judgment.
I want you to picture one school where a group of parents and teachers decided to get together and really talk about how race showed up in their community. At first, the conversations were awkward—lots of long pauses and nervous laughter. But over time, something shifted. They started sharing stories about feeling left out or finally being seen. They didn’t solve every problem overnight, but they began to see each other differently.
Here’s the key: The hardest part about talking about race isn’t the risk of saying something wrong—it’s the fear of what you might discover. But facing those fears is where real understanding starts. Silence might feel safe, but it leaves everyone alone with their questions. Conversation? Even if it’s messy, it’s the first step towards connection—and real change.
